cim: Hobby School Survey: Texans Report High Levels of Concern Over Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Hobby School Survey: Texans Report High Levels of Concern Over Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
A survey by the University of Houston's Hobby School of Public Affairs found likely voters show near universal support for requiring data center owners to pay for any required electrical grid expansion. (Credit Getty Images)

Almost eight out of 10 likely voters in Texas support limiting the number of data centers that can be built across the state, with a large majority citing concerns about the impact the massive operations have on electricity costs, water supply and the stability of the grid.

A survey of likely voters by the University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs found 79% say there should be limits on how many data centers can be built, with near universal support — 99% — for requiring those that are built to pay for any required electrical grid expansion.

The data centers needed to power the explosion of artificial intelligence and the digital economy have emerged as a potent campaign issue for the Nov. 3 election, and many candidates who previously were all in on landing the projects have tempered their support in the face of major voter concerns.

Renée Cross, professor of practice and senior executive director of the Hobby School, said voters expect data centers to bring some benefits, including technological advances and improved infrastructure for the regions in which they are built.

“Yet we also found that many voters are skeptical that the centers will have a positive impact on tax revenue and job creation, with 40% saying they will not be beneficial for job creation and 33% predicting a beneficial impact on jobs,” Cross said.

“Public officials who supported the buildout of data centers have touted the benefits for jobs, tax revenues and the overall economy, but the majority of Texas voters clearly disagree.”

—Renée Cross, senior executive director of the Hobby School

Researchers found a similar split on whether the facilities will boost tax revenues, with 33% saying they will and 38% saying they will not have a beneficial impact on tax revenues.

Three out of four voters, or 76%, say data centers will raise the cost of electricity in the communities in which they are built, while 61% say they will decrease the value of nearby homes.

“Public officials who supported the buildout of data centers have touted the benefits for jobs, tax revenues and the overall economy, but the majority of Texas voters clearly disagree,” Cross said.

Concern is highest about the impact on electricity prices, water supply and power outages, with about two out of three voters saying they are extremely or very concerned. Fewer than 20% said they are not very or not at all concerned. More than half, or 53%, say they are extremely or very concerned about the impact on noise and air pollution.

Mark P. Jones, political science fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy and senior research fellow at the Hobby School, said the concerns were consistent across demographic and geographic lines, although young voters, along with Black and Latino voters, tended to report higher levels of concern.

“The major split we saw was along partisan lines, with 93% of Democrats and 70% of independent voters saying they are very or extremely concerned about the impact on electricity prices,” he said. “Among Republicans, 51% reported those high levels of concern.”

And while 54% overall thought that artificial intelligence will hurt the economy over the next decade, compared with 37% who think it will help, that varied widely by partisanship, Jones said. Among Democrats, 81% think it will hurt the economy, and 13% think it will help, while 32% of Republicans think it will hurt the economy and 57% think it will help. Independent voters fell in the middle, with 56% saying AI will hurt the economy and 34% saying it will help.

The full report is available on the Hobby School website. The survey was fielded between Oct. 10-14 and included 2,000 Texas likely voters. The margin of error is +/-2.19%.

A future report will consider the possibility of a National Hockey League team and hockey arena in Harris County. Previous reports covered Harris County elections, statewide elections, the race for Texas Congressional District 9 and political attitudes of rural and Latino voters.
